questions.question: How did Practice Administrators expect the invite step to work?

seeded.answer:
Three out of four Practice Administrators (P154, P156, and P157) hesitated at the Invite your team step because they weren't sure when the email goes out and didn't want staff emailed before champion training is booked for the practice [1][2][3].

They didn't know whether the invite also gives staff access, or only sends the email [4].

sources.title: The Practice Administrator — Compass AI Practice Setup Journey
sources.excerpt:
Invite your team. In the test, 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P156, P157) hesitated: unsure whether the email goes out when they finish the step or at Review & finish, and not wanting staff emailed before champion training is booked for the practice. P155 entered the test staff list and went on without comment (2026-02-03 :53 ). The step used a prepared test staff list, so no real staff were emailed ( :41-42 ).
"If forty people get an email before anyone's booked training, my phone rings all afternoon." — P157 ( :64-65 )

sources.title: Wants to Know What a Step Commits Them To
sources.excerpt:
What it sends, and when. 3 of 4 Practice Administrators hesitated at Invite your team, unsure when the email goes out and not wanting staff emailed before champion training is booked ( :53 ). "If forty people get an email before anyone's booked training, my phone rings all afternoon." — P157 ( :64-65 )
What it leaves them maintaining. P159 asked whether invites create accounts or use existing SSO groups: "if it's a separate list, I'm the one keeping it in sync." ( :54 , :70-71 )

sources.title: Usability Test — Compass AI Practice Setup Flow
sources.participants: Participants: 6 — P154 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P155 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P156 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P157 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P158 — IT Administrator (it) ×1, P159 — IT Administrator (it) ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-01-20 dashboard review found setups of Compass AI for a practice stopping most at Connect calendar (7 of 24 setups started) and then at Invite your team (3 of 24), and said a dashboard can't show why ( 2026-01-20-dashboard-review-compass-ai-practice-setup-completion/session-notes.md:45-46,72 ). This session watched administrators go through the practice setup flow to find out what happens at those two steps. It is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, remote, think-aloud, 60 min/session, one participant per session
Researcher: Priya Patel (moderator)
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Participants: 6 — 4 Practice Administrators (P154-P157) and 2 IT Administrators (P158, P159)
Steps tested, in order: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO; 2 Practice details; 3 Connect calendar (read access to the practice's appointment schedule); 4 Invite your team (gives clinicians and staff access to Compass AI and sends them an email); 5 Review & finish.
Build: Steps 3 and 4 are required in this build. There is no "Connect later" and no "Skip for now"; the only way past each step is to complete it.
Design context: At session setup, the designer, Sam Okafor, stated that the calendar step is required because the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters.
Test environment: Participants signed in with their own Meridian SSO and were asked to set up as they would for their own practice. The environment was a test one: step 3 connected to a prepared sandbox calendar standing in for the practice's schedule, and step 4 used a prepared test staff list, so no real schedule was read and no real staff were emailed.
Test accommodation: When a participant stopped at step 3, the moderator told them it was the sandbox calendar and let them continue. Every participant completed step 3 this way or on their own, so completing step 3 in this session is not a result.
Not covered: The step 4 screen doesn't say when the invite email is sent, and these notes don't record when this build sends it. How Compass AI access is provisioned (through SSO groups or through these invites) wasn't known to the moderator and isn't recorded in the corpus.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (calendar: who can approve) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P155, P157) stopped at Connect calendar and wouldn't connect it: it gives Compass AI access to patient appointments, and they did not think they could approve that. Each said it was IT's decision. The fourth (P156) asked the moderator whether connecting the schedule was theirs to approve before going on. All 4 continued only on the sandbox calendar (see Test accommodation).
[MEDIUM] (calendar: what is read) Both IT Administrators (P158, P159) connected the calendar, but only after asking which fields are read (for example, whether visit reasons are included). The screen doesn't list them; the moderator couldn't answer, and both went on without an answer.
[HIGH] (invite: timing and training) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P156, P157) hesitated at Invite your team. They weren't sure whether the email goes out when they finish the step or at Review & finish, and they didn't want staff emailed before champion training is booked for the practice. P155 entered the test staff list and went on without comment.
[MEDIUM] (invite: provisioning) One IT Administrator (P159) asked whether the invites create accounts or rely on the SSO groups staff are already in. The moderator couldn't answer, and the corpus doesn't record how access is provisioned.
[LOW] (sign in and practice details) No issues at Sign in or Practice details: 6 of 6 participants completed both without help or comment on a problem.
Representative Quotes
"That's patient names and visit reasons. That's not my call — that's IT's." — Practice Administrator, P154
"Is this mine to say yes to? I'd normally send anything like this to IT." — Practice Administrator, P156
"If forty people get an email before anyone's booked training, my phone rings all afternoon." — Practice Administrator, P157
"Before I connect it I want to know what it pulls. Times and providers, fine. Visit reasons, that's a different conversation." — IT Administrator, P158
"Does this make them an account, or does it just use the groups they're already in? Because if it's a separate list, I'm the one keeping it in sync." — IT Administrator, P159
Recommendations
List the fields read from the appointment schedule on the Connect calendar step.
Add a "Send to IT for approval" path on Connect calendar for an administrator who can't approve the access themselves.
Say on the Invite your team screen when the invite email is sent.
Let administrators schedule the invite email for a date, so it can go out once training is booked.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How is Compass AI access provisioned: through SSO groups, through these invites, or both? Ask the setup flow's engineering team.
When does this build send the invite email: at step 4 or at Review & finish?
Check the setup dashboard after any copy change to these steps, to see whether setups still stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team.

"Does this make them an account, or does it just use the groups they're already in? Because if it's a separate list, I'm the one keeping it in sync." — IT Administrator, P159

Add a "Send to IT for approval" path on Connect calendar for an administrator who can't approve the access themselves.
Say on the Invite your team screen when the invite email is sent.
Let administrators schedule the invite email for a date, so it can go out once training is booked.

sources.title: Interview — Care Coordinator Supervisor on Queue Oversight
sources.participants: Participants: 1 — P132 — Care Coordinator Supervisor (care-coordinator) ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Get a care coordinator supervisor's view of what oversight they would need if alerts were AI-ranked, following up the August 2025 supervisor's concern that speed gains could mask rubber-stamping, and the override-reason capture designed after that test. The participant is a different person from P79, the supervisor in the August 2025 test.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant leads an ambulatory care coordination team. Their team works the chronological queue; the AI-ranked queue hasn't been built, and the override-reason capture wireflow is designed and in review, not built. They had not seen the August 2025 screens before; they reacted to a description of the ranked queue and the override-reason flow in this session. They did not take part in any earlier session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (oversight) If alerts were AI-ranked, they would want a record of the order each coordinator was shown and what the coordinator did with each alert, so they could look back at a case when something went wrong. They would also use override reasons for coaching, to see how a coordinator is judging risk, not only for model tuning. That raises a question the current design doesn't settle: the wireflow logs reasons for model-tuning review and says they are "not surfaced to other coordinators", but doesn't say whether supervisors see them.
[MEDIUM] (alert volume) They estimated that heavy days run "maybe 30 to 60 alerts" per coordinator, and that many of them are administrative rather than clinical. This is their informal estimate; no queue data was reviewed in this session.
[MEDIUM] (rubber-stamping) They shared the August 2025 supervisor's worry that a ranked order could be followed without judgement, but said they'd only know if it was happening by looking at what coordinators did with the order. This is a perspective, not a measurement; nothing about how often coordinators follow a ranking has been measured.
Representative Quotes
"If something goes wrong, I need to see what order they were shown and what they did with it. Otherwise I'm coaching blind." — Care Coordinator Supervisor, P132
"The reasons are the useful part for me. They tell me how someone's thinking about risk." — Care Coordinator Supervisor, P132
Recommendations
Decide who can see override reasons (model-tuning review only, or supervisors as well) before the reason-capture wireflow leaves review, and say so in the design.
If a ranked queue is piloted, record the order shown and each coordinator's action, so rubber-stamping can be looked for in data rather than assumed.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How often coordinators would follow a ranked order without judgement is not measured, and can't be until something is built and logged.
Real alert volumes per coordinator are not known; the 30 to 60 figure is one supervisor's estimate.
Whether the override-capture idea was shared with the Data Science team working on the care-gap flagging model, as the August 2025 session suggested, isn't recorded.

sources.title: Interview — Complex Care Coordinator on Alert Volume
sources.participants: Participants: 1 — P134 — Care Coordinator (complex care) (care-coordinator) ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Understand where alert noise comes from for a coordinator on a high-risk panel, and whether AI ranking addresses it, following up the August 2025 alert-triage test and the May 2026 supervisor's estimate that many alerts are administrative rather than clinical.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a care coordinator on a complex care team with a high-risk panel. Their team works the chronological queue; the AI-ranked queue hasn't been built. They reacted to a description of the ranked queue, not to screens. They did not take part in any earlier session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (repeat alerts) For them, the main source of noise is repeat alerts for the same patient, more than the order the alerts come in. They would want alerts grouped by patient before any ranking is applied, so that they deal with one patient once rather than meeting them several times down the queue. This is their account; no queue data was reviewed in this session.
[MEDIUM] (patient history) Their judgement of a patient's risk leans on knowing that patient's history, which a ranking based on the alert alone wouldn't have. This is a second voice alongside P81's 2025 comment about knowing a patient's history, from a different coordinator on a different kind of panel.
Representative Quotes
"It's not the order that gets me, it's seeing the same patient four times. Put them together first, then rank them if you want." — Care Coordinator (complex care), P134
"I know these patients. Half of deciding who's at risk is knowing what happened to them last winter." — Care Coordinator (complex care), P134
Recommendations
Explore grouping alerts by patient as a step before ranking, and test it with coordinators on high-risk panels.
Keep patient history in view when ranking signals are next revisited, in line with the August 2025 recommendation.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How many alerts are repeats for the same patient is not measured; this is one coordinator's account.
How the 2025 ranking was built and how accurate it is are still not documented, and whether the override-capture idea reached the data-science team isn't recorded.
Real-world triage speed and how often coordinators would follow a ranked order without judgement are not measured.

sources.title: Interview — New Care Coordinator on Learning the Queue
sources.participants: Participants: 1 — P135 — Care Coordinator (care-coordinator) ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Understand how a care coordinator who is new to the role learns the team's working conventions, and what an AI-ranked alert queue would mean for someone who doesn't yet have the experience to judge it, following up the August 2025 alert-triage test and the undocumented colour-coding first described in the January 2025 baseline.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a care coordinator on an ambulatory team who has been in the role for under a year. They read the signed visit notes clinicians produce, including scribe-drafted ones, but don't use the scribe themselves. Their team works the chronological queue; the AI-ranked queue hasn't been built. They reacted to a description of the ranked queue, not to screens. They did not take part in any earlier session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (learning by shadowing) They learned the team's conventions, including what the shared spreadsheet's colours mean and which alerts can safely wait, by shadowing experienced coordinators, with nothing written down to check against later. They thought a ranked queue might help newer coordinators most, because it would stand in for the judgement they haven't built yet. But they said newer coordinators would also be the least able to tell when the ranking is wrong. This is their own reflection; nothing was observed or measured in this session.
[MEDIUM] (chart review time) In their first months, chart review before an outreach call took them "closer to 20 minutes at first", which is longer than the 8-14 minutes the January 2025 baseline described for experienced coordinators. They said it has come down since. This is an informal recollection, not a timed measurement.
Representative Quotes
"Nobody gave me a list. I sat next to people for two weeks and picked up what the colours meant and which alerts could wait." — Care Coordinator, P135
"A ranked list would've been great my first month. But I wouldn't have known if it was wrong, and that's the scary part." — Care Coordinator, P135
Recommendations
Treat newer coordinators as a distinct group when the ranked queue is next tested: check whether they can spot a wrong ranking, not just whether they work faster with one.
Write down the team conventions that are currently passed on by shadowing (colour meanings, which alerts can wait), so that any design that carries or replaces them has a source to work from.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How long chart review takes for coordinators in their first year is not measured; "closer to 20 minutes at first" is one coordinator's recollection.

sources.title: Interview — New Care Coordinator on Learning the Queue
sources.participants: Participants: 1 — P135 — Care Coordinator (care-coordinator) ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Understand how a care coordinator who is new to the role learns the team's working conventions, and what an AI-ranked alert queue would mean for someone who doesn't yet have the experience to judge it, following up the August 2025 alert-triage test and the undocumented colour-coding first described in the January 2025 baseline.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a care coordinator on an ambulatory team who has been in the role for under a year. They read the signed visit notes clinicians produce, including scribe-drafted ones, but don't use the scribe themselves. Their team works the chronological queue; the AI-ranked queue hasn't been built. They reacted to a description of the ranked queue, not to screens. They did not take part in any earlier session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (learning by shadowing) They learned the team's conventions, including what the shared spreadsheet's colours mean and which alerts can safely wait, by shadowing experienced coordinators, with nothing written down to check against later. They thought a ranked queue might help newer coordinators most, because it would stand in for the judgement they haven't built yet. But they said newer coordinators would also be the least able to tell when the ranking is wrong. This is their own reflection; nothing was observed or measured in this session.
[MEDIUM] (chart review time) In their first months, chart review before an outreach call took them "closer to 20 minutes at first", which is longer than the 8-14 minutes the January 2025 baseline described for experienced coordinators. They said it has come down since. This is an informal recollection, not a timed measurement.
Representative Quotes
"Nobody gave me a list. I sat next to people for two weeks and picked up what the colours meant and which alerts could wait." — Care Coordinator, P135
"A ranked list would've been great my first month. But I wouldn't have known if it was wrong, and that's the scary part." — Care Coordinator, P135
Recommendations
Treat newer coordinators as a distinct group when the ranked queue is next tested: check whether they can spot a wrong ranking, not just whether they work faster with one.
Write down the team conventions that are currently passed on by shadowing (colour meanings, which alerts can wait), so that any design that carries or replaces them has a source to work from.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How long chart review takes for coordinators in their first year is not measured; "closer to 20 minutes at first" is one coordinator's recollection.
How accurate the 2025 ranking is, and what it was based on, are still not documented, so it isn't known how often a newer coordinator would meet a wrong ranking.
How often coordinators would follow a ranked order without their own judgement has not been measured, for newer coordinators or anyone else.

They do say that two or more clinicians use the same exam-room workstation on a clinic day, each signing in with a badge tap. Clinicians do not know what happens to their in-progress draft if a colleague signs in on that workstation while their session is locked, and they did not want to find out with a patient's visit. So they stop the scribe before leaving a room, even mid-visit, and start it again when they return. That avoids the question but splits one visit across several recordings, which they then have to read as one draft.

The sources do not say what happens to an in-progress draft when another clinician signs in on the same workstation during a lock.
They do show that a lock happens to clinicians when they step away from the workstation to the exam table within the room, typically for the physical exam, and the idle timeout fires while the scribe is listening. When they come back the widget looks frozen and shows no message. Their practice is to re-authenticate and scroll through the draft to see what is still there before they say anything more. They described learning this after re-dictating a visit summary early on and then finding the original draft intact; that is their account of their own practice, not an observed change. They put locks at "most afternoons, at least once", an informal impression.
